stature.source: typical and tall: FEIS, native trees 15-35 m, Gymnosperm Database 15-30 m; record: the tallest US tree, 48.8 m at Fortuna, California (planted, outside the native range; Gymnosperm Database); a 68.7 m planted tree in New Zealand is the world record; read 2026-11-04

targets.from: judgement values, no photographs measured: Gymnosperm Database, broadly conic when young, becoming rounded to flat; open coastal trees are broad and irregular, while closed stands keep only a shallow crown (10-20% of height)

pole.note: a young, broadly conical tree with branches low on the trunk and reddish bark

old-growth.note: an old tree (the species lives about 80-150 years) with a broad, flat-topped, wind-shaped crown, heavy limbs, grey deeply furrowed bark and dead lower branches

description: A fast-growing, short-lived pine of the foggy central coast, conical when young and later round or flat-topped and irregular. Its bright green needles come in threes, and lopsided cones stay closed on the branches for years until fire or heat opens them.

season_notes.winter: Rain-soaked and bright green; closed cones cling in whorls along the limbs.
season_notes.spring: Pale new candles stand at the branch tips and yellow pollen drifts in March.
season_notes.summer: Fog drips from the long needles, watering the ground beneath.
season_notes.fall: A few old cones split open in warm dry days and drop winged seeds.

range.where: three native fog-belt stands (Ano Nuevo in San Mateo and Santa Cruz counties, Monterey, Cambria); planted and naturalised widely in San Francisco and Marin

notes: Grown from ponderosa pine (same genus, needles in bundles, excurrent young form) with a broader, lower, irregular crown, longer and more ascending limbs, brighter green needles (Gymnosperm Database: deep yellow-green, 9-15 cm, three to a bundle) and dark, narrowly ridged bark rather than ponderosa's orange plates (red-brown when young, greying with age). The pole class keeps a young tree's conical form. What the generator cannot express: the persistent, asymmetric serotinous cones clustered on the limbs for 6-20 years (could be drawn as berries if the needle path supports them; not tried), and the wind-flagging of exposed trees. Doubt: the nearest native stand is Ano Nuevo, about 80 km south of the city; the San Francisco and Marin trees are planted, so in a world without people this species belongs on the southern edge of the region. FEIS lists birds and small mammals eating the seed and deer browsing the foliage; porcupines also take the bark but are not in the animal library.
